div.p: Background. The aim of this manuscript was to describe the frequency and types of nurse-identified needs, recommendations, and referrals delivered to intervention-arm carers of patients with high-grade glioma (HGG) during monthly nurse-led telephone assessments in the Care-IS randomized controlled trial. Methods. Primary carers of patients diagnosed with HGG (≤2 months prior) and undergoing active treatment were randomized to: a 12-month Care-IS intervention; or, a control group. Carers randomized to the intervention were included in this sub-analysis. Nurses recorded carers' needs and made recommendations and referrals. Data analysis descriptively explored categories of needs, recommendations, or referrals.

Results. An initial Nurse Telephone Assessment (NTA) was conducted with carers (N = 92) with drop-out related to time constraints, patient deterioration or death, or study withdrawal (N = 10 at month 10). Nurses identified ≥1 need, recommendation, or referral during the majority (≥90%) of NTAs. Up to 6 months, the most common needs were: dealing with treatment and side effects (74%-85%), understanding physical symptoms and side effects (60%-76%), mental and behavioral changes (53%-67%), and caring for yourself (51%-68%). The top recommendations were: tailored resources from the Care-IS resource manual (81%-96%), community-based support (47%-65%), medical specialist and clinical care (39%-56%), and additional information provision (30%-38%). The top referrals were for medical specialists and clinical care (27%-48%). Palliative care was the main recommendation (29%) and referral (19%) at months 9-10. Conclusions. NTAs identified a high frequency of carer unmet needs. Carer needs were highly variable, patientfocused, and changed over time. Nurses must accommodate a broad range of recommendations from providing additional information to making health/community referrals.

div.head: Key Points
div.p: • Carers' needs changed with time and disease progression.
• Carers of HGG patients were given regular and sustained support, information, recommendations and referrals by the nurses.
• Nurses need knowledge of a range of information and support services in the hospital and community.
Nurse-identified needs, recommendations, and referrals during consultations with family carers of patients diagnosed with high-grade glioma

div.head: Study Design
div.p: Here, we present a detailed sub-study analysis of the monthly Nurse Telephone Assessments (NTAs) conducted with carers in the Care-IS trial intervention arm only. This manuscript focuses on describing the nurse-identified needs, recommendations, and referrals for carers. Previous studies in nursing have used a similar approach to describe support provided in other areas of nursing care. 21

div.head: Care-IS Trial
div.p: Care-IS was a phase III RCT (Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registration [ACTRN] number: 12612001147875) conducted at 8 Australian sites in Perth, Western Australia (n = 3) and Sydney, New South Wales (n = 5). We have previously published the protocol, 22 feasibility testing, and refinement of the intervention, 23 analysis of the intervention effect on the primary outcome, 20 and a case study analysis of 4 highly distressed carers. 24 Ethics.-Ethics approval was granted from all sites (NSW: HREC 16/105; SJOG: 671; SCGH: 2013-172; Curtin University: HR 17/2013).

div.head: Care-IS trial: eligibility, recruitment and randomization.-
div.p: Eligible carers were the primary carers (self-identified) of a person with HGG undergoing active treatment with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or combined chemoradiotherapy, who was within 2 months of initial diagnosis.

Carers were screened for eligibility and approached before the patient started combined chemoradiotherapy by usual-care medical or nursing staff when they attended an initial appointment with the patient to discuss treatment. Referral for study participation occurred within 2 months of the initial diagnosis of grade 3/4 glioma or high-grade transformation or progression from Grade 2 Glioma.

After potential participants were identified, they were invited by a research assistant to participate and provide written informed consent. Carers who consented were randomized to receive either usual care or the nurse-led Care-IS intervention for a period of up to 12 months. 22

div.head: Importance of the Study
div.p: This study provides an understanding of the frequency and types of nurse-identified needs for carers of people diagnosed with high-grade glioma and the supporting recommendations and referrals made by nurses. Findings show the level of carer needs remained high across time and nurses needed to provide recommendation/s to most carers at monthly telephone assessments. Various carer needs were identified and nurses provided a broad range of recommendations and referrals to hospital and community services and information. The study also provides an understanding of the top categories of need, recommendations, and referrals at each time from diagnosis up to twelve months.

1082 Halkett et al.: Nurse-led support for carers of patients with HGG Care-IS nurse-led intervention.-The Care-IS intervention for carers comprised 4 parts and was delivered by a trained neuro-oncology nurse with more than 5 years of experience working in oncology or palliative care. A full description of the intervention has been previously provided. 20 In brief, a telephone assessment of the carer's unmet needs at baseline (part 1) was followed by a home visit (part 2) and delivery of a personalized hard-copy resource folder tailored to the identified unmet needs (part 3). This was followed by monthly telephone contact with the research nurse for up to 12 months (part 4). These monthly NTAs are the subject of this sub-study.

div.head: Participants
div.p: Carers randomized to the intervention arm were included if they participated in one or more NTAs during the Care-IS trial.

div.head: Nurse-led Telephone Assessments
div.p: At baseline, the research nurse contacted participants to conduct the initial telephone assessment. This was followed by a home visit (within 2 weeks) with the purpose of meeting the carer, developing rapport, and conducting an informal assessment of the carer's unmet needs. A tailored resource manual with tabbed sections relevant to the carer's needs identified during the initial telephone assessment was provided and discussed at this time.

After the initial phone call and home visit, the nurse conducted monthly NTAs for 12 months, or until the patient died or the carer withdrew. During each NTA the intervention nurse completed a patient and carer assessment and summary developed for the Care-IS trial which included questions focusing on: the patient medical summary; patient well-being; the carer's well-being; and the carer's ability to care. 20 The nurse referred to a needs classification list, identified where support was required, and subsequently documented clinical notes in an electronic study database (Microsoft Access) for each carer's monthly NTA.

The intervention nurses provided education to carers using the resource manual as well as additional publicly available education resources. Nurses were also able to recommend or make referrals for additional support (medical, allied health, practical, and supportive and psychosocial care).

div.head: Measures
div.p: Carer and patient demographic data at baseline.-Carer demographics including gender, age, relationship to the patient, education, other carer responsibilities, and employment were collected via a demographic survey completed by carers. Patient demographic data included age, gender, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status.

Nurse recorded data.-Nurses recorded call length, patient's ECOG status, 25 the number and types of needs identified, and the number and types of recommendations and referrals made during each interaction. Needs, recommendations and referral data were recorded at the level of the patient and carer dyad. The nurse also completed the validated Palliative Care -Needs Assessment Tool (PC-NAT) 26 and the Integrated Palliative Care Outcomes Scale (IPOS-5) 27 (to be reported elsewhere).

Needs identification.-Support needs specific to carers of HGG patients were categorized based on the 11 topics in the resource manual for carers. Development and evaluation of the resource manual have been previously reported. 23 The topics cover frequently identified areas of need for carers of brain tumor patients: dealing with the diagnosis; caring for yourself; practical matters; communicating with friends or relatives; communicating with health providers; dealing with treatment; understanding physical symptoms and side effects; understanding mental and behavioral changes; lifestyle choices and complementary therapies; fertility and sexuality; and end of treatment. The topics and subsections are listed in Supplementary Material 1.

div.head: Recommendations and referrals.
div.p: -Nurses addressed identified needs by providing tailored recommendations or referrals. A "recommendation" was defined as advice, suggestion, or information for the carer to implement themselves. A "referral" was defined as a nurse contact, liaison, or follow-up but did not always involve a formal written referral. Referrals were made when a need was assessed as acute or requiring clinical attention. Based on our case series analysis of distressed carers, 24 referrals, and recommendations were grouped into the following categories: allied health and specialists, community-based support, complementary medicine and spiritual care, emergency or crisis response, government or community financial support, information provision (providing additional printed information related to the need identified; refer to Supplementary Material 4 for examples), medical specialist and clinical care, mental health or psychological support, online programs/applications (recommendations only), other for example, home phlebotomist (referrals only), palliative care, provision of resources, resource manual (recommendations only), and therapies and assessments.

div.head: Data Analysis
div.p: Analysis was completed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows Version 27 (Armonk, NY: IBM Corp). To simplify the presentation of data, timepoints were collapsed by summing the number of needs, recommendations, and/or referrals for each carer for 2 adjacent timepoints: baseline and home visit (initial) and follow-up months (1 and 2; 3 and 4; 5 and 6; 7 and 8, 9, and 10). Needs, recommendations, and referrals were grouped into similar categories (see Supplements 1, 3-5) at each of these timepoints. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize and present the proportion of carers with ≥1 need, recommendation, and/or referral and the number of each at each timepoint.

In the overall cohort, the average time from recruitment to patient death was approximately 14 months. 20 Six participants did not complete any NTAs. Carer participation in NTAs declined over time due to patient death (n = 35), carers withdrawing from the study (n = 5), or time constraints or patient deterioration (n = 48). While some carers stopped participating in NTAs, some continued with other aspects of the study (ie, QoL assessment). Therefore, study withdrawal and NTA drop out are reported separately. No carers completed an NTA at 12 months. Demographic characteristics of patients and carers who received the intervention are described in Table 1. The mean age of patients was 60.4 years (SD = 11.2), the majority were male (69%), and most had an ECOG performance status of 0 (61%). Carers were aged from 28 to 85 years (M = 57.7, SD = 10.6), most were female (72%), were the spouse/partner (86%) of the patient, and 38% had children living at home. Nearly one-quarter of carers (24%) reported having experienced a significant financial effect of the diagnosis at baseline.

div.head: Summary of Descriptive Data by Month
div.p: Table 2 shows the needs, recommendations, and referrals by each month before adjacent timepoints were collapsed; month 11 is included for completeness here but is not included in the following analysis due to small numbers. During more than 90% of NTAs, nurses identified one or more needs or made recommendations or referrals. Most carers had nurse-identified need/s (highest proportion [98%] at month 1 and lowest proportion [80%] at month 10) or were given a recommendation/s (highest proportion [96%] at initial NTA and lowest proportion [73%] at month 8) at monthly NTAs. The mean number of nurse-identified needs was highest at the initial NTA (M = 11 [SD = 6.6]; range = 1-29) and lowest at month 8 (M = 3 [SD = 1.9]; range = 1-6). The mean number of recommendations was highest at the initial NTA (M = 9 [SD = 5.5]; range = 1-24) and lowest at month 7 (M = 3 [SD = 3.0]; range = 1-12). Fewer carers were given a referral at each monthly NTA compared with the proportion with a nurse-identified need or given a recommendation. The lowest proportion of carers with a referral was 21% at month 6 and the highest proportion was 50% at month 10 with the highest mean number of referrals being 3 (SD = 2.7; range = 1-10) at month 6. The longest average time taken for NTAs was 50. 5

div.head: Needs
div.p: The proportion of carers completing an NTA each month who had one or more nurse-identified needs in each category and the mean total needs are shown in Figure 1. In general, the proportion of carers with a need in most categories declined over time, with the highest proportion at initial or months 1-2 and the lowest proportion at months 7-8 or months 9-10. Conversely, the proportion of carers with needs in "dealing with treatment" and "end of treatment" increased over time from baseline to months 9-10.

The top nurse-identified needs were consistent from baseline to 6 months and included: dealing with treatment and side effects; caring for yourself; understanding physical symptoms and side effects; understanding mental and behavioral changes; and, practical matters. The most common need across months was

div.head: Neuro-Oncology
div.p: Neuro-Oncology Practice "dealing with treatment" (highest at months 1-2 [85%] and lowest at months 9-10 [57%]). A need for "lifestyle choices and complementary therapies" was identified in a small proportion of carers (≥20%) from baseline to months 7-8. By months 9-10, "end of treatment" (33%) and "dealing with the diagnosis" (33%) became 2 of the most frequently identified need categories together with "dealing with treatment" (57%), "understanding physical symptoms and side effects" (57%), "understanding mental and behavioral changes" (48%) and "caring for yourself" (38%).

Supplementary Material 3 shows a breakdown of the top 5 categories of needs at baseline including the proportion of carers identified with each need and mean number of needs. The most common needs (≥21% carers) within the "dealing with treatment" category were: fatigue, dexamethasone and its side effects, constipation, and general information about chemotherapy treatment side effects and safety precautions. The top needs within "caring for yourself" (≥24% carers) were carer strain and coping with feeling overwhelmed. Seizures, mobility issues, and preventing falls were the most common needs (≥22% carers) at baseline for "understanding physical symptoms and side effects. Learning and memory loss, personality, and behavioral changes were the top needs (≥21% of carers) for "understanding mental and behavioral changes". Loss of income and financial strain was the top need (≥23% carers) within "practical matters".

div.head: Recommendations
div.p: Figure 2 depicts the proportion of carers completing an NTA each month who received ≥1 nurse recommendation in each category and the mean total recommendations made. For most categories, the proportion of carers given a recommendation decreased over time, with the highest proportion at initial or months 1-2 and the lowest proportion at months 7-8 or months 9-10. However, the proportion of carers given recommendations in the following categories increased over time from baseline to months 9-10: palliative care, therapies and assessments, and online programs/applications. Mental health recommendations were high at baseline, lowest at months 5-6, and were high again at months 7-8 and 9-10. Emergency or crisis response recommendations followed a similar pattern, albeit at a relatively low proportion across all timepoints.

The top 6 categories of nurse recommendations from baseline to months 9-10 were: resource manual; community-based support; medical specialist and clinical care; information provision; allied health and specialists; and mental health. Palliative care was ranked equal 4 th with "information provision" at months 9-10. The top recommendation across all months was components of the resource manual tailored to needs identified (highest at baseline [96%], decreasing to 81% at months 5-6 and 76% by months 9-10).

Supplementary Material 4 shows a breakdown of the top 8 categories of recommendations at baseline including 1086 Halkett et al.: Nurse-led support for carers of patients with HGG the proportion of carers receiving each nurse recommendation and mean number of recommendations. Cancer

Council (an Australian cancer-specific charitable organization providing community support and services) was the top "community-based support" recommendation (≥52% of carers) at baseline. The highest proportion of recommendations (13%-18%) to "medical specialists and clinical care" were to: general practitioners, cancer nurse coordinators, or medical oncologists. Cancer Institute NSW brain cancer fact sheets 28 were the top recommendations within "information provision" (25% carers). The most frequent recommendations (12%-14% of carers) to "allied health and specialists" were to a: social worker, occupational therapist, or physiotherapist. The most frequent mental health recommendation was to a counselor (15% of carers) and the top "government or community financial support" recommendation (17% of carers) was Centrelink (Australian government agency for social services and payments).

div.head: Referrals
div.p: Referrals were made less frequently than recommendations, typically in response to a unique carer need identified at the time. The proportion of carers completing an NTA each month who received ≥1 nurse referral(s) in each category and the mean total referrals are shown in Figure 3. The most frequent categories for nurse referrals were consistent from baseline to months 7-8 and were to: medical specialists and clinical care; allied health and specialists; and community-based support. In months 9-10, palliative care was amongst the top 3 referrals.

The proportion of carers given a "medical specialist and clinical care" or "allied health and specialists" referral decreased over time, with the highest proportion at months 1-2 and the lowest proportion at months 7-8. Conversely, the proportion of carers given a "community-based support" or palliative care referral increased over time being highest at months 7-8 or 9-10. Mental health referrals were given to the highest proportion of carers at initial, months 1-2 and months 7-8, following a similar pattern to the recommendations. The remaining categories of referrals were needed by a very small proportion of carers, mostly within the period from baseline to months 3-4.

See Supplementary Material 5 for a breakdown of the top 4 categories of referrals at baseline including the proportion of carers receiving each type of referral and the mean number of each referral type.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: This study describes the frequency and type of unmet needs of carers of patients diagnosed with HGG which were identified by nurses in telephone assessments, along with the actions nurses took in response to those needs over a ten-month period post-diagnosis. This study expands our previous case series demonstrating the unmet needs of highly distressed carers who were receiving the Care-IS intervention. 24 The top 5 nurse-identified needs at the initial time point were: dealing with treatment; caring for yourself; understanding physical symptoms and side effects; understanding mental and behavioral changes; and practical matters. div.head: Neuro-Oncology
div.p: Neuro-Oncology Practice requiring support for these needs varied. These nurseidentified unmet needs are consistent with previous literature on the unmet needs of carers of individuals with HGG. 12,13 Analysis of the nurse-reported unmet needs, recommendations, and referrals demonstrate the breadth of clinical knowledge and the wide referral network needed by nurses engaged in providing ongoing support to this carer group. Fewer carers were given a referral at each monthly NTA compared with the proportion with a nurseidentified need or given a recommendation. Referrals were made less frequently than recommendations because the nurses used them when a need was assessed as being acute or requiring urgent clinical attention, or, there was an existing referral which had not yet been actioned by the carer and a reminder to use the service was recommended by the nurse. In this discussion we have focused on the following key areas to inform how we can best support carers of people with HGG: needs change over time; carer self-care; integration of services and disciplines; managing memory loss, mental and behavioral changes; and palliative care engagement.

div.head: Needs Change Over Time
div.p: Acknowledging that carers continue to be distressed over time 12,13 and unmet needs are evident at later time points, carers require information and support throughout the caring period. Carers may benefit from additional opportunities to discuss what to expect during treatment and their role in supporting the patient to manage symptoms and side effects at home. These information needs remained high as patients received a range of treatment and physical symptoms and side effects changed over time. A number of tools are available to assist clinical teams in screening patients and carers for unmet needs following a brain tumor diagnosis. For example, Chen et al. 29 developed a brief unmet need screening tool for carers of people with a brain tumor. Additionally, Campbell et al. 30 have developed a brief screening measure for unmet supportive care needs for people with HGG that could be administered routinely. Furthermore, Faris et al. 31 recently defined criteria for 4 levels of unmet needs of patients diagnosed with HGG for use in a stepped care pathway. This approach may assist in identifying and managing unmet needs and referring patients within the health system and community. Further research should investigate how healthcare professionals could support carers during medical appointments and attend to their unmet needs particularly anticipating how needs may evolve or new needs arise as the disease progresses.

div.head: Carer Self-care
div.p: Carer self-care remained in the top 3 nurse-identified needs over time. During NTAs nurses discussed the importance of carers looking after themselves and maintaining their own well-being. Previous research has reported carers of people with advanced illness struggle to look after their own needs 32 while prioritizing the needs of the person with HGG. 33 Additionally, in a recent systematic scoping review, Hart et al. 34 found some carers have difficulty balancing their needs with those of a person with advanced cancer. 1088 Halkett et al.: Nurse-led support for carers of patients with HGG

Coyne et al. 35 have developed video resources in Australia for carers to assist in reducing the burden of caring for a person with brain cancer. Additionally, Whisenant et al. 36 recently piloted simulation-based caregiving skills training for family members of HGG patients demonstrating this training was acceptable and perceived useful by 10 carers in the USA.

div.head: Integration of Services and Disciplines
div.p: Our analysis of nurse recommendations demonstrates the breadth of the information and support carers required, highlighting nurses' need to be knowledgeable about a comprehensive range of services available both in the hospital and community, as well as paths to access those services. Familiarity must cover neuro-oncology treatment, allied health, in-home services, written resources, and psycho-oncology services. The European Cancer Organization proposed frameworks and recommendations for quality cancer care for adult glioma, stating multidisciplinary teamwork and collaboration were essential, and that teams should be organized around one key worker who assesses patients' needs and develops care plans with the patient. 37 The Australian Optimal Care Pathway for all people affected by HGG, both patients and carers, advocates for shared care between the treating specialist and a primary care provider or suitably qualified nurse. 38 Involvement of primary care providers has been demonstrated to improve the survival of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, and initiation and completion of adjuvant treatment 39 and nurses coordinating care around patient needs may provide similar benefits. In the Care-IS study, follow-up appointments enabled nurses to assess carers' levels of distress and needs and inform and support carers as the patient's disease progressed.

div.head: Managing Memory Loss, Mental, and Behavioral Changes
div.p: During the delivery of the intervention, nurses spent time providing information and support to carers to help them understand and manage memory loss, as well as mental and behavioral changes experienced by the person with HGG. Additionally, nurses made recommendations and referrals to community-based support, medical specialists, allied health, and mental health professionals to assist carers in the management of these changes. McDougall et al. 40 scoping review highlighted few interventions have been tested for the management of brain tumor-related personality and behavior changes. The NICE guidelines for brain tumors 41 highlight fluctuating neurological symptoms over the disease course. A neuropsychological assessment may be beneficial for understanding the neurocognitive deficits underlying these changes. There is no specific time when neurorehabilitation is definitively required as people's experiences of HGG differ. Thus, regular check-ins and screening for personality and behavioral changes with patients and their carers should be considered at all follow-up stages, along with the provision of information about contributing factors to changes and referrals for neuropsychological assessment and management when required.

div.head: Palliative Care Engagement
div.p: Recommendations and referrals for palliative care became more important/common for carers at later timepoints as the patient's health declined. Although referral to palliative care during diagnosis or treatment can benefit people with HGG and improve survival, studies have found that only approximately 1 in 10 patients are referred early after diagnosis due to health system barriers and patient and carer perceptions that palliative care means the end of life. 42,43 In a recent survey of 103 people with cancer in Australia, Chosich et al. 44 reported that 40% felt frightened and 29% felt hopeless about referral to palliative care. Clinicians should consider early referral to palliative care, during treatment or at diagnosis, as it can improve quality of life. 38 If referral is based on need rather than prognosis as recommended, this may help to overcome patient and carer biases against palliative care and increase engagement.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: The overall Care-IS RCT limited recruitment to Englishspeaking carers living in 2 Australian states. The RCT had a substantial drop-out over time in both groups, as expected for this poor prognosis tumor type. Carers of patients with Grade 3 or Grade 4 HGG were eligible to participate in this study. Although the experience of a Grade 3 and Grade 4 tumor can be different, this difference was not explored in the main RCT analysis. While the data presented were collected as part of an RCT, the nurse-collected data was part of the intervention, thus this analysis does not involve a comparison to the control group. Additionally, we are unable to report on the needs of those who did not continue with NTAs when the patient further declined or died as the Care-IS intervention did not provide ongoing support for bereaved carers. The descriptive data presented here are from nurse assessments and reporting and may not represent the full extent of the patient and carer's needs. Patients were often present during the home visit which added to the nurse's understanding of the carer's situation; however, at times it prevented carers from talking freely about all their needs. Although nurses asked carers about previously identified needs at each NTA, we did not routinely collect data on the uptake of recommendations and referrals and acknowledge there may be financial, logistical, or time barriers which prevented patients and carers from accessing the nurse recommended or referred services.

div.head: Implications for Practice
div.p: Nurses supporting carers of people with HGG need to be skilled in eliciting and advising on a variety of needs, ranging from treatment side effects and physical symptoms to behavioral and mental health concerns; from complementary therapies through to allied health and palliative care. Nurses need to understand the availability and access pathways for a broad range of services from hospital-based

div.head: Neuro-Oncology
div.p: Neuro-Oncology Practice and external health providers to community organizations. The training needs of nurses providing this care should be considered.

Table 3 provides a summary of recommendations for management for areas of high unmet needs based on the top 5 nurse-identified unmet needs in this study. In addition to providing information to carers, health services need to support neuro-oncology nursing/coordinator positions to deliver or provide access to supportive care for neuro-oncology patients and their carers. Additional community-based support is likely to also be beneficial to support carers from diagnosis through to the end of life.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This study demonstrates the frequency, nature, and breadth of nurse-identified unmet needs of carers of patients diagnosed with HGG. To address these needs, nurses provided recommendations and referrals to a range of services in the hospital and community setting. Health professionals providing this level of support for carers require neuro-oncology-focused education and training to be able to skillfully provide such a breadth of information, support, and referral to adjunct services.

div.head: Table 3. Recommendations for Clinical Practice for Areas of High Unmet Carer Need
div.p: Nurse-identified areas of unmet need Recommendations for clinical practice Dealing with treatment As most treatment for HGG, after surgery, is delivered in the outpatient or community setting, patients and carers should be regularly assessed by a nurse/allied health professional (eg, monthly as was done in this study), to deliver timely support to them in managing side effects of treatment alongside changes associated with disease progression.

Caring for yourself Carers should be asked how they are coping and offered regular support for their emotional and physical well-being and to maintain self-care strategies over time. Provide education about the potential for carer strain and normalize help-seeking/ accessing supports.

div.head: Physical symptoms and side effects
div.p: Carers and patients should be given regular education and information tailored to their health literacy level to help them understand physical symptoms and side effects. Health education videos for carers and family may be useful to reinforce concepts and provide carers with information on their role in providing support and managing symptoms. Health education videos may be more accessible than written resources.

Understanding mental and behavioral changes Carers require ongoing support and tailored information (e.g., contributing factors to changes including tumor location, treatment side effects, emotional adjustment to diagnosis, etc) to assist them in understanding mental and behavioral changes experienced by people with HGG. Referral for additional support and neurorehabilitation may be beneficial for some people with HGG and their carers.

div.head: Practical matters
div.p: In the initial period after diagnosis, carers require support for their practical needs such as income loss, financial strain, transport, ethical and legal matters. These needs highlight the importance of social work involvement.

div.head: End of treatment
div.p: In light of the poor prognosis of HGG, early involvement of palliative care services is likely to be beneficial to both the patient and carer.
